questions.stem:
A mass of 8.0 g oscillates in simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 5.0 mm at a frequency of 40 Hz.

What is the total energy of this simple harmonic oscillator?
questions.stemText: A mass of 8.0 g oscillates in simple harmonic motion with an amplitude of 5.0 mm at a frequency of 40 Hz. What is the total energy of this simple harmonic oscillator? A 0.16 mJ B 6.3 mJ C 13 mJ D 640 mJ

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into the SHM energy formula with unit conversions.
questions.misconception: Using frequency f instead of angular frequency ω

perOption.A: Uses $\omega = f$ instead of $\omega = 2\pi f$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Omits the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
perOption.D: Uses an amplitude of 5.0 cm instead of 5.0 mm.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
When a cork is pushed down into still water in a tank and then released, it oscillates with simple harmonic motion of period 0.12 s.

Water waves are then set up in the tank and its frequency adjusted until the cork is observed to have a maximum amplitude of vibration.

The speed v of the water waves is given by

where g is the acceleration due to gravity and d is the depth of the water in the tank.

If the depth of the water in the tank is 0.30 m, what is the wavelength of the water waves when the cork is moving up and down with the largest amplitude?
questions.stemText: When a cork is pushed down into still water in a tank and then released, it oscillates with simple harmonic motion of period 0.12 s. Water waves are then set up in the tank and its frequency adjusted until the cork is observed to have a maximum amplitude of vibration. The speed v of the water waves is given by = v gd where g is the acceleration due to gravity and d is the depth of the water in the tank. If the depth of the water in the tank is 0.30 m, what is the wavelength of the water waves when the cork is moving up and down with the largest amplitude? A 0.070 m B 0.14 m C 0.21 m D 0.35 m

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must link resonance to the natural frequency and then combine with a given wave-speed formula.
questions.misconception: Not recognising that maximum amplitude means driving frequency equals natural frequency

explanation.body:
The cork vibrates with maximum amplitude at resonance, when the wave period equals the cork's natural period, $T = 0.12$ s.

$v = \sqrt{gd} = \dfrac{\lambda}{T}$, so $\lambda = T\sqrt{gd} = 0.12\sqrt{9.81\times0.30} = 0.206\ \mathrm{m} \approx 0.21\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from $\lambda = vT$ with $v = \sqrt{gd}$.
perOption.C: Correct. Resonance: wave period equals the natural period.
perOption.D: Forgets the square root: $Tgd \approx 0.35$ m.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion along a line with a maximum speed $v_0$. What is the speed of the particle when the displacement of the particle is half of its amplitude? A $\frac{1}{4}v_0$ B $\frac{1}{2}v_0$ C $\frac{3}{4}v_0$ D $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}v_0$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion along a line with a maximum speed v0. What is the speed of the particle when the displacement of the particle

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Direct substitution into $v = \omega\sqrt{x_0^2 - x^2}$.
questions.misconception: Assuming speed varies linearly with displacement

explanation.body: At half the amplitude $x_0$, the speed is $v=\omega\sqrt{x_0^2-x_0^2/4}$. This simplifies to $v=(\sqrt{3}/2)\omega x_0=(\sqrt{3}/2)v_0$.

perOption.A: Uses the squared displacement fraction as the speed fraction.
perOption.B: Assumes halving the displacement halves the speed.
perOption.C: Uses the fraction of squared speed without taking its square root.
perOption.D: Correct. The speed is $\sqrt{3}/2$ times its maximum.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation, with time t, of the acceleration a of the particle from t = 0 to t = 2 s.

Which graph could represent the variation, with time t, of the kinetic energy of the particle from t = 0 to t = 2 s?
questions.stemText: A particle oscillates with simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation, with time t, of the acceleration a of the particle from t = 0 to t = 2 s. a 0 0 2 t/s Which graph could represent the variation, with time t, of the kinetic energy of the particle from t = 0 to t = 2 s? A kinetic energy 0 0 t/s 2 B kinetic energy 0 0 t/s 2 C kinetic energy 0 0 t/s 2 D kinetic energy 0 0 t/s 2

appearances.originalFile: CJC PHY/H2/J2.H2.PRELIM.2026.Paper 1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs phase reasoning from a to x to v and recognising KE has half the period.
questions.misconception: Forgetting that kinetic energy oscillates at twice the frequency of displacement

explanation.body: At $t=0$, acceleration is zero, so the particle is at equilibrium and its kinetic energy is maximum. Acceleration is zero three times from $t=0$ to $2\ \mathrm s$ inclusive, so the kinetic energy has three maxima in that interval.

perOption.A: Misses the kinetic-energy peak at the middle equilibrium crossing.
perOption.B: Shows zero kinetic energy at the initial and final equilibrium crossings.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Puts kinetic-energy minima at the equilibrium crossings.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: A small mass on a vibrating platform undergoes simple harmonic motion. The total energy of the mass is 18 mJ. The amplitude of the oscillation is now doubled, and the time period is increased to be three times as long. What is the new total energy of the mass?
questions.stemText: A small mass on a vibrating platform undergoes simple harmonic motion. The total energy of the mass is 18 mJ. The amplitude of the oscillation is now doubled, and the time period is increased to be three times as long. What is the new total energy of the mass? A 8 mJ B 12 mJ C 36 mJ D 72 mJ

appearances.originalFile: DHS Physics Prelim 2026/H2/DHS 2026 Y6 Physics H2 P1 Prelim (for external sharing).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Two simultaneous scaling factors in $E = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_0^2$.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the period change or not squaring ω

explanation.body: The total energy is $E=\tfrac12mv_0^2=\tfrac12m(\omega x_0)^2$, so $E\propto(x_0/T)^2$. Doubling $x_0$ and tripling $T$ gives $E_{\mathrm{new}}/E_{\mathrm{old}}=(2/3)^2=4/9$. The new energy is $(4/9)(18\ \mathrm{mJ})=8\ \mathrm{mJ}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Applies the factor of $2/3$ without squaring it.
perOption.C: Doubles the energy directly and ignores the change in period.
perOption.D: Squares the amplitude factor but ignores the longer period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText: Bodies X and Y performs simple harmonic motion. Body Y has twice the mass of body X and oscillates with half the amplitude. The maximum acceleration of body Y is three times that of body X. What is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{total energy of body Y}}{\text{total energy of body X}}$? A 1.5 B 2.0 C 3.0 D 6.0

stemImage.alt: Question 14: Bodies X and Y performs simple harmonic motion. Body Y has twice the mass of body X and oscillates with half the amplitude. The maximum acceleration of body Y i

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Must combine $a_0 = \omega^2x_0$ and $E = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2x_0^2$ with three ratios.
questions.misconception: Assuming the same angular frequency for both bodies

explanation.body: In SHM the maximum acceleration has magnitude $\omega^2 A$. Thus $3=(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2(0.5)$, so $(\omega_Y/\omega_X)^2=6$. Using $E=\tfrac12 m\omega^2 A^2$, the energy ratio is $2(6)(0.5)^2=3.0$.

perOption.A: Omits the doubling of the mass.
perOption.B: Uses only the mass ratio and ignores the changes in angular frequency and amplitude.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses the amplitude ratio to the first power in the energy expression.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A pendulum with a period of 2.0 s starts its swing from its extreme position.

How long does it take to reach halfway between its extreme position and equilibrium position?
questions.stemText: A pendulum with a period of 2.0 s starts its swing from its extreme position. How long does it take to reach halfway between its extreme position and equilibrium position? A 0.17 s B 0.25 s C 0.33 s D 1.0 s

appearances.originalFile: JPJC PHYSICS/H2/2026 Prelim H2 Phy P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires choosing the cosine form and solving for phase, not assuming linear motion.
questions.misconception: Assuming the bob moves at constant speed so half the distance takes half the time

explanation.body: Starting at the extreme position gives $x=A\cos(2\pi t/T)$. At the halfway point, $0.5A=A\cos[(2\pi/2.0)t]$. The first solution is $t=0.33\ \mathrm{s}$.

perOption.A: Uses a sine equation with zero initial displacement, as if the pendulum started at equilibrium.
perOption.B: Assumes the pendulum covers half the distance to equilibrium in half the time.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Uses half a period, when the pendulum reaches the opposite extreme.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A car is driven over a series of equally spaced bumps separated by a distance of 5.0 m.

If the natural frequency of the car’s suspension system is 2.0 Hz, what is the speed of the car for it to experience a large amplitude of vibration?
questions.stemText: A car is driven over a series of equally spaced bumps separated by a distance of 5.0 m. If the natural frequency of the car’s suspension system is 2.0 Hz, what is the speed of the car for it to experience a large amplitude of vibration? A 1.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ B 2.5 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ C 5.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ D 10 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Resonance condition plus a single speed = distance × frequency step.
questions.misconception: Dividing frequency by spacing (or spacing by frequency) instead of multiplying

explanation.body: For resonance, the frequency of hitting the bumps equals the suspension’s natural frequency. The time between bumps is $T=1/2.0=0.50\ \mathrm{s}$. Using $d=vT$ gives $5.0=v(0.50)$, so $v=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: This speed gives one bump every $5.0\ \mathrm{s}$, so the driving frequency is too low.
perOption.B: Multiplies by the period instead of dividing the spacing by it.
perOption.C: This speed gives one bump per second, only half the natural frequency.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which statement is true of a lightly-damped system?
questions.stemText: Which statement is true of a lightly-damped system? A Increasing the damping will decrease the frequency of the system. B Increasing the damping will not affect the period of the system. C The amplitude of the system remains constant over time. D The period of the system increases over time.

options.label: A
options.text: Increasing the damping will decrease the frequency of the system.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the damping will not affect the period of the system.

options.label: C
options.text: The amplitude of the system remains constant over time.

options.label: D
options.text: The period of the system increases over time.

appearances.originalFile: MI Physics/H2/2026 PU3 H2 PHYSICS PRELIM P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing that damping lowers the oscillation frequency, which students often ignore for light damping.
questions.misconception: Believing damping has no effect on the period, or that the period changes as amplitude decays

explanation.body: Increasing the damping decreases the oscillation frequency and therefore increases the period. With the damping held fixed, the amplitude decreases over time while the period stays constant.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Increasing the damping increases the period because the frequency falls.
perOption.C: Damping dissipates energy, so the amplitude decreases over time.
perOption.D: At fixed damping the period stays constant as the amplitude decays.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A particle moves such that its acceleration a is related to its displacement x from a fixed point as shown.

What is its angular frequency?
questions.stemText: A particle moves such that its acceleration a is related to its displacement x from a fixed point as shown. a / cms2 0.30 6.0 x / cm 0 6.0 0.30 What is its angular frequency? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: NJC/H2 Physics/NJC_2026_H2_Physics_Prelim_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Reading the gradient of an a–x graph and taking a square root.
questions.misconception: Forgetting to square-root the gradient to get ω

explanation.body: For simple harmonic motion, the acceleration and displacement amplitudes obey $a_0=\omega^2x_0$. The graph gives $0.30\times10^{-2}=\omega^2(6.0\times10^{-2})$, so $\omega=0.22\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

perOption.A: Uses $\omega^2$ directly as the angular frequency.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Takes the square root of the reciprocal ratio $x_0/a_0$.
perOption.D: Uses $x_0/a_0$ and also omits the square root.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A body is undergoing undamped oscillations that are simple harmonic. A graph of the variation of displacement x of the body with time t is shown.

Which graph shows the variation of the kinetic energy E of the body with time t?
questions.stemText: A body is undergoing undamped oscillations that are simple harmonic. A graph of the variation of displacement x of the body with time t is shown. Which graph shows the variation of the kinetic energy E of the body with time t? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: NYJC/H2/2026 NYJC H2 Phy 9478 P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Needs linking x = 0 at t = 0 to maximum KE and recognising KE never goes negative and has twice the frequency.
questions.misconception: Plotting KE with the same shape and frequency as displacement

explanation.body: At $t=0$, the body is at equilibrium ($x=0$), where its speed and kinetic energy are greatest. It passes through equilibrium twice per oscillation, so the kinetic energy completes two cycles in one displacement period.

perOption.A: Copies the displacement graph and gives negative kinetic energy.
perOption.B: Uses a signed velocity-like curve, which gives negative kinetic energy.
perOption.C: Starts at zero even though the body has maximum speed at equilibrium.
perOption.D: Correct. It starts at a maximum and repeats every half-period.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A student models a playground swing as a simple harmonic oscillator moving along a straight horizontal path directly above a scale.

The extreme positions reached by the swing correspond to the 0 m mark and the 2.00 m mark on the scale.

If the period of oscillation of the swing is 2.4 s, how long does it take for the swing to travel directly from the 0.75 m mark to the 1.50 m mark?
questions.stemText: A student models a playground swing as a simple harmonic oscillator moving along a straight horizontal path directly above a scale. The extreme positions reached by the swing correspond to the 0 m mark and the 2.00 m mark on the scale. If the period of oscillation of the swing is 2.4 s, how long does it take for the swing to travel directly from the 0.75 m mark to the 1.50 m mark? A 0.30 s B 0.40 s C 0.50 s D 0.90 s

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must convert scale readings into displacements from equilibrium and solve two inverse-cosine equations.
questions.misconception: Measuring displacement from the end of the scale rather than from equilibrium

explanation.body:
Amplitude $x_0 = \dfrac{2.00}{2} = 1.00\ \mathrm{m}$, with the equilibrium position at the 1.00 m mark. So the 0.75 m mark is at $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$ and the 1.50 m mark is at $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.

Taking the swing to be at the 0 m mark at $t = 0$: $x = -1.00\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{2.4}t\right)$

At $x = -0.25\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_1 = 0.5035\ \mathrm{s}$. At $x = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$: $t_2 = 0.8000\ \mathrm{s}$.

Time taken $= t_2 - t_1 = 0.8000 - 0.5035 = 0.2965 \approx 0.30\ \mathrm{s}$

perOption.A: Correct. $t_2 - t_1$ from $x = -x_0\cos\omega t$.
perOption.B: Does not come from applying $x = -x_0\cos\omega t$ to the correct displacements, $-0.25$ m and $+0.50$ m.
perOption.C: Gives roughly $t_1$, the time from the 0 m mark to the 0.75 m mark, instead of the time between the two marks.
perOption.D: Does not come from the sinusoidal relation. The whole journey from 0 m to 1.50 m takes only 0.80 s.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A body oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation with displacement $x$ of the velocity $v$ of the body.

[Graph: $v$ / m s$^{-1}$ against $x$ / m is an ellipse centred at the origin, crossing the $x$-axis at $-0.50$ and $0.50$ and the $v$-axis at $2.0$ and $-2.0$.]

The body is now made to oscillate such that its amplitude is reduced to 0.25 m, while maintaining the same total mechanical energy.

What is the new maximum acceleration of the body?

A $4.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   B $8.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   C $16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$   D $32\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

stemImage.alt: Question 13: A body oscillates in simple harmonic motion. The graph shows the variation with displacement x of the velocity v of the body. v / m s−1 2.0 x / m 0 −0.50 0.50 −

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must read $x_0$ and $v_0$ from the ellipse and realise that constant energy forces $\omega$ to change.
questions.misconception: Assuming the angular frequency stays the same when the amplitude changes

explanation.body:
From the graph, $x_0 = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ and $v_0 = 2.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $\omega = \dfrac{v_0}{x_0} = \dfrac{2.0}{0.50} = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

Total energy $E_T = \tfrac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x_0^2$. Since $E_T$ and $m$ are constant, $\omega x_0$ stays constant:

$\omega' x_0' = \omega x_0 \Rightarrow \omega' = \dfrac{4.0 \times 0.50}{0.25} = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$

$|a_0| = (\omega')^2 x_0' = 8.0^2 \times 0.25 = 16\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$

perOption.A: Keeps $\omega = 4.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ unchanged and uses the new amplitude: $4.0^2 \times 0.25$.
perOption.B: Gives the original maximum acceleration, $4.0^2 \times 0.50$.
perOption.C: Correct. Constant energy keeps $\omega x_0$ fixed, so $\omega$ doubles.
perOption.D: Uses the new $\omega' = 8.0\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$ with the old amplitude of 0.50 m.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A mass hanging from a spring suspended from the ceiling is pulled down and released. The mass then oscillates vertically with simple harmonic motion of period $T$. The graph shows how its distance from the ceiling varies with time $t$.

[Graph of distance from ceiling / cm against $t$. The curve starts at $100\ \mathrm{cm}$ at $t=0$ with a horizontal tangent, falls most steeply at $t=T/4$, and levels off at $30\ \mathrm{cm}$ at $t=T/2$. Dashed guides mark $T/4$, $T/2$ and $30\ \mathrm{cm}$. Both axes show zero.]

What can be deduced from this graph?

A  The amplitude of the oscillation is 70 cm.
B  The kinetic energy is a maximum at $t=\frac{T}{2}$.
C  The restoring force on the mass increases between $t=0$ and $t=\frac{T}{4}$.
D  The speed is a maximum at $t=\frac{T}{4}$.

stemImage.alt: Question 15: A mass hanging from a spring suspended from the ceiling is pulled down and released. The mass then oscillates vertically with simple harmonic motion of period T

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Read the positions of equilibrium and the turning points from the graph.
questions.misconception: Taking the peak-to-peak distance as the amplitude

explanation.body: The mass is at one extreme at $t=0$, passes through equilibrium at $t=T/4$, and reaches the other extreme at $t=T/2$. Its speed is greatest at equilibrium, so it is a maximum at $t=T/4$.

perOption.A: The $70\ \mathrm{cm}$ is the peak-to-peak distance, giving an amplitude of $35\ \mathrm{cm}$.
perOption.B: At $t=T/2$ the mass is at a turning point, so its speed and kinetic energy are zero.
perOption.C: The magnitude of the restoring force falls to zero as the mass approaches equilibrium.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object undergoes a simple harmonic motion with an amplitude $A$, and its total energy is $E$.

What is the displacement of the object from the equilibrium position when its kinetic energy is $\frac{3E}{4}$?

A  $\frac{A}{4}$
B  $\frac{A}{2}$
C  $\frac{3A}{4}$
D  $\frac{A\sqrt{3}}{2}$

stemImage.alt: Question 16: An object undergoes a simple harmonic motion with an amplitude A, and its total energy is E. What is the displacement of the object from the equilibrium positio

appearances.originalFile: RVHS/RVHS H2 Physics P1 QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Substitute the total energy into the kinetic energy expression and solve for displacement.
questions.misconception: Treating energy as linear in displacement

explanation.body: The total energy is $E=\tfrac12m\omega^2A^2$, and the kinetic energy is $E_k=\tfrac12m\omega^2(A^2-x^2)$. Substituting $E_k=\tfrac34 E$ gives $\tfrac34A^2=A^2-x^2$. Thus the displacement has magnitude $|x|=A/2$.

perOption.A: This treats the potential energy fraction $1/4$ as a displacement fraction.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This treats the kinetic energy fraction $3/4$ as a displacement fraction.
perOption.D: This assigns the fraction $3/4$ to potential energy.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A particle is moving such that the force-displacement on it changes with the distance $r$ from a fixed point as shown.

[The force–displacement graph is a straight line with negative gradient through the origin.]

Which energy-displacement graph shows the potential energy (p.e.) and kinetic energy (k.e.) correctly?

A [An upward-opening p.e. parabola has its minimum at zero displacement. A downward-opening k.e. parabola has its maximum there.]
B [The same curves as A, with the k.e. and p.e. labels swapped.]
C [The p.e. has a minimum and the k.e. has a maximum at zero displacement. Both curves flatten toward the ends of the displacement range.]
D [The same curves as C, with the k.e. and p.e. labels swapped.]

stemImage.alt: Question 12: A particle is moving such that the force-displacement on it changes with the distance r from a fixed point as shown. Which energy-displacement graph shows the p

appearances.originalFile: SAJC - note P3 will be used for mock on 6 oct/2026 SAJC H2 Physics Prelim P1_for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires identifying simple harmonic motion from the force graph and recognising the quadratic energy dependence.
questions.misconception: Assuming any two curves with constant total energy fit SHM

explanation.body: The straight force–displacement line through the origin has negative gradient, so the motion is simple harmonic. Its kinetic energy is $K=\tfrac12mv^2=\tfrac12m\omega^2(x_0^2-x^2)$, an inverted parabola with a maximum at $x=0$. Total energy $K+U$ is constant, so potential energy rises quadratically as kinetic energy falls.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Swaps kinetic and potential energy, placing minimum kinetic energy at equilibrium.
perOption.C: Places maximum kinetic energy at equilibrium but gives it the wrong, non-parabolic shape.
perOption.D: Places minimum kinetic energy at equilibrium and gives it a non-parabolic shape.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An oscillator is forced to oscillate at different frequencies. The graph of amplitude A against driving frequency f for this oscillator is shown.

The damping on the oscillator is now decreased.

Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1 The amplitude of the oscillations at any frequency decreases. 2 The maximum amplitude occurs at a lower frequency. 3 The peak on the graph becomes sharper.
questions.stemText: An oscillator is forced to oscillate at different frequencies. The graph of amplitude A against driving frequency f for this oscillator is shown. The damping on the oscillator is now decreased. Which of the following statements is/are correct? 1 The amplitude of the oscillations at any frequency decreases. 2 The maximum amplitude occurs at a lower frequency. 3 The peak on the graph becomes sharper. A Only 1 B Only 2 C Only 3 D 1, 2 and 3

appearances.originalFile: TJC/H2 Physics/2026 H2 Prelim Paper 1 final.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must distinguish changes in peak height, width and frequency.
questions.misconception: Reducing damping shifts resonance to a lower frequency.

explanation.body: Reducing damping reduces energy loss, increasing the amplitude near resonance. The resonance peak narrows and shifts towards the undamped natural frequency, which is higher than the damped peak frequency. Only statement 3 is correct.

perOption.A: Statement 1 reverses the effect of lower damping on the amplitude near resonance.
perOption.B: Statement 2 reverses the shift of the peak frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Includes statements 1 and 2, which reverse the changes in amplitude and peak frequency.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A particle is oscillating in simple harmonic motion. The kinetic energy of the particle is $E_{\mathrm K}$, its potential energy is $E_{\mathrm P}$ and the total energy is $E_{\mathrm T}$. When the particle is mid-way between the equilibrium position and an amplitude position, what are the values of the ratios $E_{\mathrm K}:E_{\mathrm T}$ and $E_{\mathrm P}:E_{\mathrm T}$?
[Table columns are $E_{\mathrm K}:E_{\mathrm T}$ and $E_{\mathrm P}:E_{\mathrm T}$.]
A $1:4$, $3:4$
B $1:2$, $1:2$
C $2:3$, $1:3$
D $3:4$, $1:4$

stemImage.alt: Question 11: A particle is oscillating in simple harmonic motion. The kinetic energy of the particle is EK, its potential energy is EP and the total energy is ET. When the p

appearances.originalFile: TMJC/TMJC_2026_H2 Physics_P1_QP.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: It requires evaluating the kinetic-energy fraction at half amplitude and finding the remaining fraction.
questions.misconception: Assuming energy varies linearly with displacement

explanation.body: For amplitude $x_0$, the total energy is $E_{\mathrm T}=\frac12m\omega^2x_0^2$. At $x=x_0/2$, $E_{\mathrm K}=\frac12m\omega^2[x_0^2-(x_0/2)^2]=\frac34E_{\mathrm T}$. Since $E_{\mathrm T}=E_{\mathrm K}+E_{\mathrm P}$, $E_{\mathrm P}=\frac14E_{\mathrm T}$.

perOption.A: Interchanges the kinetic and potential energy fractions.
perOption.B: Assumes the energies are equal halfway to the turning point.
perOption.C: Overestimates the potential-energy fraction, which is $(x/x_0)^2=1/4$.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText:
The diagram shows the graph of displacement against time for a body performing simple harmonic motion. At which time, A, B, C or D is the body travelling and accelerating in the opposite direction?

[The displacement–time graph starts near a positive maximum, falls through zero, reaches a negative minimum and rises back through zero towards a positive maximum. A is on the descending curve above zero, B is at the descending zero crossing, C is on the descending curve below zero and D is at the negative minimum.]

questions.difficultyReason: The student must compare the slope of the displacement graph with the direction of the restoring acceleration.
questions.misconception: Reading the sign of displacement as the sign of acceleration.

explanation.body: The displacement curve starts at its positive maximum, so velocity follows a negative sine curve and acceleration follows a negative cosine curve. At C the velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive, so the body is travelling and accelerating in opposite directions.

perOption.A: Velocity and acceleration are both negative.
perOption.B: Acceleration is zero as the body passes through equilibrium.
perOption.C: Correct. The velocity is negative and the acceleration is positive.
perOption.D: Velocity is zero at the turning point.

questions.stem:
A particle of mass 4.0 kg moves with simple harmonic motion and its potential energy U varies with position x as shown in the figure below.

What is the period of oscillation of the particle?
questions.stemText: A particle of mass 4.0 kg moves with simple harmonic motion and its potential energy U varies with position x as shown in the figure below. What is the period of oscillation of the particle? A 0.25 s B 0.89 s C 1.8 s D 2.5 s

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must read an energy–position pair and connect it to angular frequency and period.
questions.misconception: Using the full horizontal span as the displacement.

explanation.body: From the graph, $U=1.0\ \mathrm{J}$ at $x=0.2\ \mathrm{m}$. Using the SHM energy relation and $\omega=2\pi/T$ gives $1.0=\tfrac12(4.0)(2\pi/T)^2(0.2)^2$. Solving gives $T=1.78\ \mathrm{s}$, or $1.8\ \mathrm{s}$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Gives a period that predicts a potential energy far above 1.0 J at the marked displacement.
perOption.B: Halves the calculated full period.
perOption.C: Correct. The energy–position pair gives a period of about 1.8 s.
perOption.D: Is consistent with omitting the factor of one half in the energy formula.

Two identical simple pendulums P and Q in different environments are given the same initial displacement and are then released. The graphs show the variation with time t of their displacements x.

P and Q are then subjected to driving forces of the same constant amplitude and of variable frequency f. Which graph represents the variation with f of the amplitudes A of P and of Q?
questions.stemText: Two identical simple pendulums P and Q in different environments are given the same initial displacement and are then released. The graphs show the variation with time t of their displacements x. P and Q are then subjected to driving forces of the same constant amplitude and of variable frequency f. Which graph represents the variation with f of the amplitudes A of P and of Q? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires inferring relative damping from free oscillations and applying it to forced response curves.
questions.misconception: Expecting stronger damping to raise the resonance peak.

explanation.body: Q's free oscillations die away faster, so Q is more strongly damped. Its frequency-response curve lies below P's at positive driving frequencies, which rules out A and B. Q has a lower peak at a slightly lower frequency than P.

perOption.A: Shows Q above P over parts of the frequency range.
perOption.B: Shows Q crossing above P and peaking at a higher frequency.
perOption.C: Correct.
perOption.D: Gives the more strongly damped Q a taller peak.
